newsitem.title: USA: Mellon sale to allow focus on core units.
newsitem.headline: Mellon sale to allow focus on core units.

text.p: Mellon Bank Corp's intention to sell its corporate trust business reflects a growing trend of consolidation in that arena that has narrowed the field of players and will allow Mellon to focus assets on core businesses, analysts said Friday.
The planned sale, which was announced Friday, is expected to have a minimal impact on earnings.
"Banks are focusing themselves on the businesses in which they are major players," said Ronald Mandle at Sanford C. Bernstein.

Mellon said earlier Friday it intends to sell its corporate trust business, which includes corporate trustee, registrar, paying agent and escrow agent services for corporate, municipal, state and institutional bond issues.
Mellon's corporate trust portfolio comprises 6,600 accounts with outstanding debt of $70 billion.
Analysts said the unit represents a very minor portion of Mellon's overall fudiciary business, contributing only about $0.02 per share to earnings.

"(A sale) will have (a very small effect) on Mellon's earnings," said David Hilder at Morgan Stanley. "The implication of this is Mellon realized that although it was one of the 10 largest providers of corporate trust services, it was not sufficient enough to build a profitable, long-term and growing business.
"They realized it was better to sell the business than remain in it."
Mellon shares were down 1-7/8 to 73-1/8 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

A Mellon spokesman declined to comment on a selling price but analysts said the business would likely sell between $60 and $80 million. The company said in a news release that a transaction could be concluded in the third or fourth quarter.

"This is a business that represents about $25 to $30 million in revenues. It's not a core business for them," said Jim Schutz at The Chicago Corp. "I think (Mellon) realized that in order to remain competitive in that business, they would have to allocate an awful lot of capital funds."
Indeed, Frank Cahouet, Mellon's chairman, said in the news release that in order to keep its corporate trust business competitive, Mellon would have had to invest too heavily.

"Corporate trust is a business that is driven by scale, with increasingly intense competition among a narrowing group of major providers," he said. "We have concluded that continuing to successfully provide a competitive service...will require an additional investment that is not consistent with our core strategy or financial objectives."
The corporate trust business has been consolidating during the 1990s. Several banks have sold those businesses to other banks that in turn have become increasingly larger players.
Analysts said the major players, including Bank of New York Co Inc, State Street Boston Corp, and First Bank System could be potential buyers for Mellon's corporate trust unit.
"I'd be surprised if they weren't (considering it) right now," Schutz said.
Officials from those companies were unavailable for comment.
